conversation.content:
Good morning! I’m Claire, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually shortened to the EPDS. It’s a quick, 10-question check-in that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally and physically during the past seven days of new motherhood. Everything you share stays between you and the care team; there’s no right or wrong answer, and many parents find it reassuring to put words to what they’re experiencing. When you’re ready, we’ll move through each question together at your pace.

Let’s begin: Over the last seven days, have you still been able to look forward with enjoyment to things, or has that been difficult for you?

I still want to enjoy things—like when my sister brought over coffee and held the baby so I could finish a whole cup while it was still hot—but even that felt kind of flat. I *want* to look forward to little pleasures, but mostly they feel muted, like I’m watching myself do them rather than really feeling the happiness.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Sometimes a little giggle slips out—like when the baby does a big milk-drunk grin—but it feels forced, like I have to remind myself, “This is cute, you should laugh.” Most of the time the humor just falls flat.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I try—every night I tell myself, “Tomorrow I’ll enjoy that walk with the stroller” or “I’ll actually like my coffee again”—but when morning comes, it’s like the color’s been drained out of everything. I still *plan* for nice moments, but the spark I used to feel beforehand is barely there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… if the baby spits up a lot or won’t settle, my brain jumps straight to “I must be doing something wrong.” I know rationally that babies just cry and spit up, but I still catch myself thinking I’m failing him somehow. It’s not every second of the day, but it pops up several times and leaves me feeling lousy.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly picture him choking, or I’ll hear a siren and imagine it’s because something happened to my husband. I know the odds are tiny, but the thoughts show up anyway and they loop until I force myself to check the baby three extra times.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A couple of times this week my heart just started racing—like I was about to walk into traffic—except I was only folding onesies on the couch. It hits fast, I feel shaky and short-of-breath, and then it fades, but I’m left wired and watching the baby monitor like something awful might happen.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. I’ll look at the sink full of bottles, the laundry mountain, and the baby fussing, and feel like I’m drowning. I still push through, but it’s like I’m operating on autopilot—just ticking boxes until bedtime, then lying awake thinking about tomorrow’s list.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. I’ll finally get him down, crawl into bed myself, and then my mind starts spinning—replaying every tiny thing I did “wrong,” picturing worst-case scenarios. It takes me an hour or more to drift off, and when I do wake up for his feeding I can’t fall back because the anxious loop starts again.
I have felt sad or miserable

That pretty much sums most days up. It’s like a gray cloud parked over me—I can still smile at the baby or answer a text, but underneath I just feel heavy and weepy. Some afternoons I end up crying while I rock him, even when nothing specific happened.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened twice this week. Yesterday I was warming up a bottle and just started bawling—no real trigger, just this wave of sadness that wouldn’t quit. It lasts maybe ten minutes, then I wipe my face and keep going, but it leaves me exhausted.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

It crossed my mind once or twice—like a fleeting picture of not being here anymore—but I don’t have any plan and I know I’d never leave my baby. Still, the idea popped up when I felt really overwhelmed and ashamed for not coping better.

Listening to you, I hear how hard you're working to stay afloat while your days feel colorless and heavy. Your love for your baby shines through, yet sadness, worry, and a sense of drowning have taken over most moments, and sleep offers little relief.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only occasional, forced laughter and that humor "falls flat" most of the time, aligning with "Definitely not so much now."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent loss of anticipatory joy ('spark ... barely there'), matching 'Hardly at all'.</sym>, <sym>She endorses self-blame "several times" a day, matching "Yes, some of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports daily intrusive catastrophic thoughts that recur and compel checking behaviors, indicating very frequent anxiety without cause.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic episodes with physical symptoms and persistent dread, matching the highest frequency option.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling overwhelmed "most days" and describes functioning on autopilot, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports nightly sleep-onset delay >1h plus middle-of-night return of racing anxious thoughts, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive sadness ("most days", "gray cloud", "heavy and weepy") and frequent crying, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes two sudden crying episodes this week, consistent with "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes the self-harm thought occurring "once or twice" as "fleeting", aligning with the "Sometimes" option.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 25/30 plus Item 10 ≥1 places you well above the 14-point cutoff indicating probable major <med>depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med> and co-occurring <med>anxiety</med>. You endorse core symptoms: depressed mood most days (<quote>gray cloud</quote>), marked <sym>anhedonia</sym> (<quote>spark...barely there</quote>), <sym>guilt</sym>, <sym>sleep disturbance</sym>, <sym>feeling overwhelmed</sym>, <sym>panic-like episodes</sym>, and fleeting <sym>self-harm ideation</sym>, meeting <med>DSM-5</med> threshold. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or perinatal psychiatrist
2. Request formal <med>depression</med> and <med>anxiety</med> evaluation plus safety assessment
3. Ask about evidence-based treatments: <med>CBT</med>, <med>IPT</med>, or sertraline compatible with breastfeeding
4. Plan daily 15-minute support (partner/friend) to allow rest breaks and reduce stimulation
5. Practice 4-7-8 breathing when panic sensations start; keep lights dim during night feeds
6. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to track progress
7. If thoughts of self-harm intensify, call 988 (US) or your local emergency number immediately
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note

Patient-reported symptoms (10-item EPDS-style):
- Persistent low mood, frequent tearfulness, feelings of “heaviness”
- Marked loss of enjoyment/anticipation (“color drained out of everything”)
- Excessive self-blame and guilt regarding infant care
- Daily, intrusive anxious worries (infant safety, catastrophic images)
- Episodic panic-type sensations (heart racing, shakiness) without clear trigger
- Feeling overwhelmed/drowning most days; functioning on “autopilot”
- Initial and return sleep disturbance driven by rumination and worry
- Passive, non-specific self-harm ideation (no plan or intent); endorsed as fleeting when overwhelmed

Pattern: symptoms present most days, interfere with sleep and coping, no current psychosis or mania reported.

Screening significance
- Meets threshold indicators for probable major depressive episode with peripartum onset and comorbid anxiety
- Safety concern: presence of self-harm thoughts (passive) warrants formal risk assessment and safety planning

Risk factors identified
- Guilt/self-criticism, pervasive sadness, anhedonia, panic symptoms, sleep loss, passive suicidal ideation

Next step
- Refer for immediate comprehensive psychiatric evaluation and safety assessment; consider expedited outpatient or intensive perinatal mental-health services.
